country.comment: Fieldwork focuses on the Ganakatuli (also spelled Ganaktuli) Sweeper Colony in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title; PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 6, Methodology

effect_estimate.comment: Quantitative results are purely descriptive percentages, midpoint approximations, and benchmarked arithmetic gaps (including a 50 percentage-point water access deficit and a 64.4% service deficit index); no inferential statistical tests, CIs, p-values, or regression models linking tenure or administrative variables to water/sanitation outcomes are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive statistics and qualitative findings only (no inferential regression, CI, or p-value reported): 35% of colony households have piped/clean water access vs. 85% national average (50 percentage-point water access deficit), 85% live in 100 sq. ft. single-room dwellings (16.67 sq. ft./person) with shared sanitation facilities, and only 15% hold legal land/property documents (outside the colony); qualitatively, municipal urban planning neglect, unfulfilled post-2018 colony rehabilitation housing, and city corporation salary deductions for utilities without issuing official utility bills in residents' names perpetuate service and civic exclusion
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 8, Case Study; PDF pp. 9–11, Results and Statistical Analysis, Tables 1–3

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <=2 by non-experimental mixed-methods design. Coded as 1 because piped water access (35%) and shared sanitation (85%) are presented as descriptive colony-level statistics alongside low legal tenure (15%) and benchmarked against national averages, while direct qualitative observation of administrative mechanisms (municipal utility deductions without official bills in residents' names, unallocated rebuilt rehabilitation quarters, ignored boundary-wall requests, and circumvented job quotas) documents civic/passport verification, housing, and employment barriers rather than directly tracing administrative decisions operating on water or sanitation access.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 4–5, Historical Roots & Literature Review; PDF p. 8, Case Study; PDF p. 10, Table 3

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines lack of land/property tenure documents (15% legal tenure), absence of official utility bills in residents' names despite municipal salary deductions and stigma tied to colony address on voter ID (documentation), neglect of sweeper colonies in municipal urban planning and unfulfilled post-2018 housing rehabilitation (planning), administrative implementation gaps and political favoritism despite constitutional guarantees and quotas (discretion), and exclusion of Harijans and Harijan women from urban governance and decision-making (participation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, documentation, tenure, property, planning, discretion, participation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 3–5, Introduction, Historical Roots & Literature Review; PDF pp. 7–8, Methodology & Case Study; PDF pp. 10–11, Table 3 & Discussion

outcome_flags.comment: Measures household access to clean/piped water (35%), reliance on shared sanitation facilities in overcrowded one-room dwellings (85%), and colony-level water/service coverage deficits relative to national coverage (50 percentage-point water access deficit and 64.4% service deficit index).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 9–11, Results and Statistical Analysis, Table 3

sample_size.comment: Abstract and Methodology state n=150 surveyed households (38% Hindu Harijans, 62% Muslim Cleaners), n=30 interviews, and 3 FGDs (8–10 participants each), whereas the Results text mentions 5 FGDs and Tables 1–2 report colony-wide figures across 1,494 households (563 Hindu Harijan and 931 Muslim Cleaner households; 8,867 individuals).
sample_size.value: 150 households (150 survey respondents aged 30–70), 30 in-depth/key-stakeholder interviews, and 3 focus group discussions of 8–10 participants each (reported as 5 FGDs in Results); Results tables also report 1,494 households / 8,867 individuals
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 6–7, Methodology; PDF pp. 8–10, Results and Statistical Analysis, Tables 1–2

study_design.comment: Six-month mixed-methods fieldwork (March–August 2023) using purposive and snowball sampling, analyzed via descriptive statistics (SPSS/Excel) and qualitative thematic analysis (NVivo), without a quasi-experimental or regression-based causal identification strategy.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods case study combining a cross-sectional structured household survey (descriptive statistics) with qualitative in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, participant observation, and secondary census/policy review
